extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in screenwriting, film students, aspiring or working screenwriters, and general readers of film industry memoirs
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and teach practical screenwriting craft and the realities of working in Hollywood through essays, project case studies, a worked adaptation, screenplay texts, and interviews with industry figures. Useful for learning how to begin/end scripts, write for stars, adapt prose, and analyze screenplay strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hollywood Realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Part One: 'Hollywood Realities' is a collection of essays on various subjects ranging from movie stars and studio executives to his thoughts on how to begin and end a screenplay and how to write for a movie star.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section frames practical, real-world considerations of the American film industry—relationships with stars and executives, and how industry context shapes writing choices. Presented as essays rather than formal rules, useful for understanding the environment in which a screenplay must function.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to begin and end a screenplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman's 'thoughts on how to begin and end a screenplay'—advice on openings and endings for scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contained in Part One as prose guidance; implies evaluative criteria for effective openings and conclusions (how a screenplay should start and finish). The book presents these as craft observations from experience rather than formalized checklist items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for a movie star
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on 'how to write for a movie star'—tailoring screenplay elements to suit star personas and careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in Part One alongside industry realities; the guidance implies criteria for character and dialogue choices, role emphasis, and structure when a script is meant to showcase or accommodate a star.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project case studies (Adventures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part Two: 'Adventures' contains stories from 11 projects Goldman was involved with, from Charly and Masquerade to Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid and All the President's Men, and some unrealized projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These case studies serve as models for evaluating what worked or failed on real projects; they provide concrete examples and lessons drawn from actual screenwriting and production histories, useful for deriving practical criteria (e.g., adaptation choices, collaboration pitfalls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting a short story into a screenplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Part Three: Goldman demonstrates 'how he would go about adapting his own short story "Da Vinci" into a screenplay', including the full text of the short story and the subsequent screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a worked example of the adaptation process—useful as an evaluative benchmark for assessing adaptation choices (what to keep, expand, condense, or change), structure, and fidelity versus screen needs. The inclusion of both source text and resulting screenplay gives side-by-side comparison opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screenplay analysis — identifying strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The expanded edition includes the full screenplay of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid plus Goldman's analysis of the screenplay's strengths and weaknesses (presented as 'Part Three' in that edition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides explicit critique and commentary on a canonical screenplay; serves as an exemplar for how to analyze a screenplay's elements and articulate what constitutes strengths or weaknesses in plot, character, pacing, and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry perspectives through interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: The book includes interviews with key movie industry figures (e.g., director George Roy Hill, cinematographer Gordon Willis, composer Dave Grusin) following the Da Vinci adaptation section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interviews add practitioner's perspectives on filmmaking craft and decision-making; they act as auxiliary evaluative input about how different collaborators assess screenplay and production choices, useful for understanding multi-disciplinary criteria.
